title: Autosomal Recessive Disorders in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance means both alleles must be mutated for disease. In low‑resource settings, consanguinity, endemic infections and limited testing shape diagnosis and management.

sections.p: AR disorders arise when a child inherits two pathogenic variants. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, family history, and confirmatory tests such as genetic panels or biochemical assays.

t.b: Identifies pathogenic variants; positive result confirms AR inheritance
Detects abnormal metabolites; a pattern suggests a specific AR metabolic disease

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and functional impact. For many metabolic disorders, the Wilson‑Bennett or MIM criteria are used; for haemoglobinopathies, the WHO severity scale applies.
b: Mild: asymptomatic or single organ involvement
Severe: multisystem failure or early death

sections.p: In East Africa, the top AR causes are sickle cell disease, β‑thalassemia, cystic fibrosis, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and lysosomal storage disorders. Infections such as malaria can unmask or worsen these conditions.

t.b: Detects abnormal hemoglobin variants; confirms sickle cell or thalassemia
Elevated in congenital adrenal hyperplasia; indicates enzyme deficiency

sections.p: Presentation varies with organ system. Common clues include failure to thrive, recurrent infections, jaundice, bone pain, and easy bruising. A detailed history of consanguinity and family disease is essential.
b: Failure to thrive and growth retardation

t.b: Palpable spleen >2 cm below costal margin suggests hemolytic anemia or storage disease
May indicate chronic hemolysis or iron overload

sections.p: Start with basic labs; use point‑of‑care tests where possible. When advanced tests are unavailable, clinical criteria guide management.

t.b: Differentiates microcytic anemia (thalassemia) from normocytic (sickle cell) and identifies target cells
Elevated in iron overload; supports diagnosis of haemochromatosis or transfusion‑related iron overload

sections.p: Urgent signs include severe anemia, hypoxia, acute chest syndrome, or liver failure. Complications such as stroke, organ failure, or infections can be fatal if untreated.

t.b: Low SpO2 (<90%) indicates hypoxia; urgent intervention needed
Detects hepatomegaly or cirrhosis; guides management of storage diseases

sections.p: Treat the underlying defect, provide supportive care, and monitor for complications. Drug choice balances efficacy, availability, and safety in low‑resource settings.
b: Hydroxyurea for sickle cell to reduce crises
Enzyme replacement for lysosomal storage when available

t.b: Increases fetal hemoglobin; reduces vaso‑occlusive episodes
Treats adrenal crisis; replaces deficient cortisol

sections.p: Regular monitoring of organ function, vaccination, and genetic counselling are key. Prevention focuses on reducing consanguinity and early newborn screening.

t.b: Early detection allows prophylaxis with penicillin and vaccination

sections.p: Many AR disorders mimic common infections or nutritional deficiencies. Distinguish by specific laboratory patterns and family history.

t.b: Target cells suggest thalassemia; schistocytes suggest hemolysis

sections.p: Low‑resource labs may give false negatives; for example, ferritin can be normal in early iron overload. Clinical context is essential.
b: Serum ferritin may be normal early in haemochromatosis
Hemoglobin electrophoresis may miss rare variants

t.b: If clinical suspicion remains high, repeat the test or use a different method

faq.q: How do I differentiate sickle cell from malaria in a febrile child?
faq.a: Look for sickle cells on smear, persistent anemia, and a history of vaso‑occlusive crises; malaria shows parasites and may have splenomegaly but not sickle cells.

faq.q: What is the first step if a child has suspected cystic fibrosis but no sweat chloride machine?
faq.a: Use clinical criteria: recurrent pneumonia, failure to thrive, and a positive newborn screen if available; refer for genetic testing if possible.

faq.q: Why is hydroxyurea preferred over transfusion in sickle cell?
faq.a: It reduces crises, is cheaper, and avoids iron overload and alloimmunisation; transfusion is reserved for acute severe cases.

exam: A 6‑month‑old boy from a consanguineous family presents with failure to thrive and pallor. What is the most likely diagnosis and first test? — Sickle cell disease; hemoglobin electrophoresis. A child with recurrent chest infections and nasal polyps is found to have a positive sweat chloride test. What is the next step? — Confirm CFTR mutation; start pancreatic enzyme replacement.
